usage: Tool/means takes -으로 after a consonant: 노트북 ends in ㄱ, so 노트북으로, never 노트북로.
The on/off pair is 켜다/끄다; for booting you also hear 부팅하다, but 켜다 is the everyday word.
가볍다 (light) vs 무겁다 (heavy) is the standard weight pair buyers care about; 가벼워요 is the ㅂ-irregular polite form.
충전(充電) 'fill electricity'; you charge the 배터리, and when it dies you say 배터리가 다 됐어요.
examples: 이 노트북 가벼워요.
This laptop is light.
Simple description; 가볍다 is a ㅂ-irregular, so polite form is 가벼워요, not 가볍어요.
노트북으로 영화도 봐요.
I watch movies on my laptop too.
도 'also' attaches to the object to add it to other uses; note the means particle 으로 on the device.
회사에서 노트북을 한 대 줬어요.
The company gave me a laptop.
Computers and machines are counted with the counter 대, so 한 대 = one (machine).
nuance: 노트북 is the default Korean word for a laptop computer — it comes from English 'notebook' (short for 노트북 컴퓨터), so a beginner's instinct that it means a paper notebook is the classic 직역 trap: a paper notebook is 공책 or just 노트, and only the computer is 노트북. The near-synonym 컴퓨터 is the umbrella term for any computer, while 노트북 specifically marks the portable/foldable kind; a desktop is 데스크톱 or 데스크탑. 랩탑 exists as a transliteration but sounds foreign and is rarely spoken — Koreans say 노트북. Register is fully neutral, fine in any setting. Habitual collocations: 노트북을 켜다/끄다 (turn on/off), 노트북으로 일하다/공부하다 (work/study on it), 노트북이 느리다/빠르다, 가볍다/무겁다, and 노트북을 충전하다 (charge it). The pitfall for English speakers is the particle: 'on a laptop' is 노트북으로 (means), not 노트북에 — 노트북에 would mean physically 'onto/in the laptop' (e.g. saving a file).

mistakes: Saying 랩탑 because it matches English 'laptop'. It is understood but sounds unnatural — Koreans overwhelmingly say 노트북.
Using 노트북 for a paper notebook. A spiral paper notebook is 공책 or 노트; 노트북 is only the computer. 'I wrote in my 노트북' would sound like you typed into a laptop.
Writing 노트북에서 영화를 봐요 for 'I watch movies on a laptop'. The device as a means takes 으로 (노트북으로 영화를 봐요); 에서 marks a location, so it implies the movie is somewhere inside the device.

usage: 마우스 ends in a vowel (ㅡ→스), and the rule still gives 마우스로; 클릭하다 borrows 'click' + 하다.
고장 나다 = 'a breakdown occurs', the natural way to say a device stopped working; spaced 고장 나다.
움직이다 is the everyday verb for moving an object slightly; 마우스를 움직여요 in polite speech.
무선(無線) 'no-wire'; the opposite wired is 유선(有線), so 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스.
examples: 마우스가 안 돼요.
The mouse isn't working.
안 되다 'doesn't work/function' is how you report a device problem in casual speech.
마우스로 그림도 그려요.
I even draw pictures with the mouse.
도 adds drawing as an extra use; 그리다 (draw) → 그려요.
새 마우스를 하나 샀어요.
I bought a new mouse.
Small countable items use 하나 (one) naturally; 새 (new) goes directly before the noun.
nuance: 마우스 is purely the computer pointing device — it is a transliteration of English 'mouse' and, crucially, never means the animal. The live animal is 쥐 (which covers both mice and rats; Korean does not split them the way English does), so the English habit of one word for both is exactly the pitfall: '쥐가 고장 났어요' would be absurd, and '마우스가 집에 있어요' sounds like hardware, not a pet. Register is neutral and technical-everyday. Natural collocations: 마우스로 클릭하다 (click), 마우스를 움직이다 (move it), 마우스가 고장 나다 / 안 되다 (it breaks / doesn't work), and the wired/wireless split 유선 마우스 vs 무선 마우스. The means particle is again 으로 — 마우스로 클릭하다, not 마우스에 클릭하다 (English 'click ON' tempts 에/에서, but Korean treats the mouse as the instrument, so 으로).

mistakes: Using 마우스 for the animal. The rodent is 쥐; 마우스 only ever means the computer device.
Saying 마우스에 클릭해요 by analogy with 'click ON the mouse'. You click WITH the mouse, so it's the instrument: 마우스로 클릭해요. 클릭하다 itself takes the screen target with 을/를 or just the place you click.
Expecting a separate word for a small mouse vs a big rat in everyday talk — Korean uses 쥐 for both, so don't search for a 마우스/쥐 size distinction the way English has mouse/rat.

usage: to watch a movie on a monitor
Means particle 으로 marks the screen you view it through; 보다 (watch) → 봐요.
Size pair 크다 (big) / 작다 (small); 화면(畫面) 'screen' is the display surface, so 화면이 크다 is also common.
연결(連結) 'link-tie'; you 연결하다 (connect) a monitor to a 노트북 with a 케이블.
Borrowed 듀얼 'dual'; two screens side by side, very common phrasing in offices: 모니터 두 대.
examples: 모니터가 너무 밝아요.
The monitor is too bright.
너무 'too (much)' before an adjective; 밝다 (bright) → 밝아요.
모니터로 사진을 크게 봐요.
I view photos large on the monitor.
크게 is the adverb form of 크다 'big' → 'largely/in big size'.
큰 모니터를 한 대 사고 싶어요.
I want to buy a big monitor.
Screens are machines, so counter 대; -고 싶다 expresses the speaker's own desire.
nuance: 모니터 is specifically a computer display screen, distinct from a 텔레비전/TV which is a broadcast set you watch programs on — the dividing line is function, not shape: even an identical-looking panel is a 모니터 if it shows your computer and a 텔레비전 if it receives channels. From English 'monitor', it stays neutral in register. Note the related word 화면 (畫面, 'picture-surface') means the screen/display *content or surface* itself, so '화면이 꺼졌어요' = the display went dark, while '모니터를 샀어요' = I bought the physical unit. Habitual collocations: 모니터를 켜다/끄다, 모니터로 ~를 보다, 모니터를 연결하다 (connect), 모니터가 크다/작다/밝다/어둡다, and 듀얼 모니터 / 모니터 두 대. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a TV a 모니터 (and vice versa), plus reaching for 에서 — you watch 모니터로 (through it as a means), and 모니터에 means onto the monitor (e.g. 모니터에 먼지가 있어요, dust on the monitor).

mistakes: Calling a television a 모니터. A TV that receives channels is 텔레비전 (or TV); 모니터 is the computer screen only.
Mixing up 모니터 and 화면. 모니터 is the physical device; 화면 is the screen surface/picture. '화면이 안 나와요' = no picture is showing, which is about the display, not the box.
Saying 모니터에서 영화를 봐요 for watching via the monitor. Use 모니터로 (by means of the monitor); 에서 marks a location and sounds like the movie lives inside the device.

usage: The machine is 프린터; the action is 인쇄(印刷)하다 'print'. 프린트하다 (from 'print') also exists colloquially.
고장 나다 for a malfunction; office printers famously 자주 고장 나요 (break down often).
the printer is out of paper
에 marks the container/location here — paper is inside the printer, so 프린터에, not 프린터로.
흑백(黑白) 'black-white'; color is 컬러, so 컬러 프린터 vs 흑백 프린터.
examples: 프린터로 사진을 뽑아요.
I print photos with the printer.
뽑다 'pull out/print out' is the casual verb for getting a printout; means particle 으로.
회사에 프린터가 한 대 있어요.
There is a printer at the office.
Existence 있다 with location 에; machines counted with 대.
프린터에 종이가 다 떨어졌어요.
The printer ran out of paper.
다 떨어지다 'be all used up'; 에 marks where the paper is (inside the printer).
nuance: 프린터 is the physical printing machine (from English 'printer'), and the key contrast learners must internalize is device vs action: the act of printing is 인쇄하다 (印刷하다, Sino-Korean 'print') or casually 프린트하다 / 뽑다, while a printed handout itself is 프린트 (a 프린트, a printout). So '프린터를 했어요' is wrong — you 인쇄를 했어요 (did the printing) using the 프린터. Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 프린터로 인쇄하다/뽑다, 프린터가 고장 나다, 프린터에 종이가 없다/떨어지다, 프린터로 ~를 출력하다 (출력 出力, the more technical 'output/print'), and 컬러/흑백 프린터. Two particle traps: the means is 프린터로 (print *with* it), but supplies live *in* it, so paper and ink take 에 — 프린터에 종이가 없어요, 프린터에 잉크가 떨어졌어요. English 'print it on the printer' wrongly suggests 에 for the action.

Using 프린터로 종이가 없어요 for 'out of paper'. The paper is inside the machine, so use 에: 프린터에 종이가 없어요. Reserve 으로 for the printing action itself.

usage: to listen to music on a speaker
Means 으로; 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular → 들어요 (the ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel).
소리 'sound', 크다 'big/loud'; for sound, 크다/작다 = loud/quiet, so 소리가 커요.
켜다/끄다 on/off; a Bluetooth speaker you 블루투스로 연결하다 (connect via Bluetooth) first.
블루투스 'Bluetooth'; wireless portable ones are everywhere, phrased 블루투스 스피커.
examples: 스피커 소리가 너무 커요.
The speaker is too loud.
Sound volume uses 크다 (loud) / 작다 (quiet), not 시끄럽다 here; 시끄럽다 is 'noisy/annoying'.
스피커로 노래를 틀어요.
I play songs on the speaker.
틀다 'turn on/play (audio/video)' is the natural verb for playing music; means particle 으로.
새 스피커를 하나 샀어요.
I bought a new speaker.
하나 for one small item; 새 directly before the noun for 'new'.
nuance: 스피커 (from English 'speaker') means the audio output device that plays sound — and the trap is that, unlike English, it does NOT mean a person speaking. A speaker at an event/lecture is 발표자 (發表者, 'presenter') or 연사 (演士), and a native speaker of a language is 원어민; calling a presenter a 스피커 is a 직역 mistake. Register is neutral, technical-everyday. Useful contrast: 스피커 outputs sound out loud, whereas 이어폰/헤드폰 send it privately to your ears. Habitual collocations: 스피커로 음악을 듣다/틀다, 스피커를 켜다/끄다, 스피커 소리가 크다/작다, 스피커를 (블루투스로) 연결하다, and 블루투스 스피커. For volume use 소리가 크다/작다 (loud/quiet), and note 음량/볼륨 (volume) is the level you 높이다/낮추다 (raise/lower). The particle pitfall: play music 스피커로 (means), not 스피커에서.

Saying 스피커가 시끄러워요 to mean 'the speaker is loud'. 시끄럽다 means 'noisy/bothersome'. For plain loudness say 소리가 커요; use 시끄럽다 only when the sound is annoying.
Saying 스피커에서 음악을 들어요 for listening via the speaker. The device is the means: 스피커로 음악을 들어요. 에서 marks a place and sounds odd here.

usage: to listen to music with earphones
Means 으로 after consonant ㄴ; 이어폰으로. Listening is 듣다 → 들어요 (ㄷ-irregular).
끼다 'insert/wear (snug things)' is the verb for in-ear buds; 끼다/빼다 = put in / take out.
줄 'cord/wire'; 엉키다 'get tangled'. Wired buds are 유선 이어폰.
무선(無線) 'wireless'; the true-wireless buds (like AirPods) are 무선 이어폰 or 블루투스 이어폰.
examples: 이어폰을 끼고 음악을 들어요.
I put in earphones and listen to music.
-고 links two actions in sequence; 끼다 is the right verb for in-ear buds (not 쓰다/입다).
지하철에서는 이어폰을 써요.
On the subway I use earphones.
Here 쓰다 'use' is fine for the general act of using; 에서는 = at (location) + topic 는.
이어폰 줄이 자꾸 엉켜요.
The earphone cord keeps tangling.
자꾸 'repeatedly/keep ~ing' captures the recurring annoyance; 엉키다 → 엉켜요.
nuance: 이어폰 (from 'earphone') are small in-ear listening devices, and the sharp contrast is with 헤드폰 — the bigger over-the-ear cans: don't call headphones 이어폰. Within earbuds, wired ones are 유선 이어폰 and the true-wireless type (AirPods-style) are 무선 이어폰 / 블루투스 이어폰, though many people just say 에어팟 generically. Register is neutral. The verb pitfall is choosing how to 'wear' them: in-ear buds take 끼다 (insert snugly) — 이어폰을 끼다 — while over-ear 헤드폰 take 쓰다 (wear on the head); 입다 (wear clothes) is wrong for both. Habitual collocations: 이어폰을 끼다/빼다, 이어폰으로 음악을/영어를 듣다, 이어폰 줄이 엉키다, and 무선/유선 이어폰. Particle note: listen 이어폰으로 (means), and the cord 줄 takes 이/가 as the subject that tangles (줄이 엉켜요), not 을/를.

Saying 이어폰을 입다 or 이어폰을 신다 for putting them in. In-ear buds take 끼다 (이어폰을 끼다). 입다 is for clothing and 신다 is for footwear.
Using 이어폰에서 음악을 들어요. The earphones are the means, so 이어폰으로 음악을 들어요. Reserve 에서 for a location, not a device you listen through.

usage: Means 으로; mobile data as the means of connecting. 데이터로 = on (mobile) data.
부족(不足)하다 'be insufficient'; near month-end people say 데이터가 부족해요.
to use up all the data
다 'all' + 쓰다 'use'; 데이터를 다 썼어요 = the allowance is gone.
무제한(無制限) 'no-limit'; a 데이터 무제한 요금제 is an unlimited-data plan.
examples: 이번 달 데이터가 부족해요.
I'm low on data this month.
이번 달 'this month' sets the time frame; 부족하다 'be insufficient/short'.
와이파이가 없어서 데이터를 써요.
I use data because there's no wifi.
-아서/어서 gives reason; 없어서 'because there isn't', then the result clause.
데이터를 다 써서 영상이 안 나와요.
I used up my data, so videos won't play.
Chained -아서/어서 for cause; 안 나오다 'won't come out/play' for media not loading.
nuance: 데이터 (from English 'data') in everyday Korean almost always means your mobile-phone data allowance, not abstract research information — that everyday narrowing is the pitfall: a scientist's 'the data shows...' is 자료 (資料, 'reference material') or 데이터 in technical writing, but '데이터가 없어요' to a normal person means your phone's data ran out, not 'there is no information.' The near-synonym is 정보 (情報, 'information'), which is the content/knowledge itself, distinct from the data allowance you buy. Register is neutral and very common when newcomers set up a phone. Habitual collocations: 데이터를 쓰다/다 쓰다, 데이터가 부족하다/남다 (be short / be left over), 데이터로 영상을 보다, 데이터를 켜다/끄다 (toggle mobile data), and 데이터 무제한 (unlimited). Particle pitfall: connect 데이터로 (by means of data), not 데이터에서. Also, 'a lot of data' is 데이터가 많다, and 'out of data' is 데이터가 떨어지다/다 되다.

mistakes: Equating 데이터 with 정보 in daily talk. To a normal person 데이터 = your phone's data allowance; abstract information is 정보, and research data is 자료.

Using 데이터가 없어요 to mean 'there is no information'. To most listeners that means your mobile data is used up. For 'no information' say 정보가 없어요.

usage: to switch to a new plan
바꾸다 'change/switch'; the target plan takes 으로 (요금제로 바꾸다) = 'change INTO a plan'.
고르다 'pick' is a 르-irregular → 골라요; you compare and 고르다 a 요금제.
비싸다 (expensive) / 싸다 (cheap) is the price pair; 비싸요/싸요 in polite speech.
A 요금제 named by its feature; 무제한(無制限) 'no-limit', a very common plan type.
examples: 싼 요금제로 바꾸고 싶어요.
I want to switch to a cheaper plan.
Target of 바꾸다 takes 으로; -고 싶다 for the speaker's wish.
이 요금제는 데이터가 많아요.
This plan has a lot of data.
Topic 는 introduces the plan, then comments on its data; 많다 'be a lot' → 많아요.
요금제 좀 추천해 주세요.
Could you recommend a plan?
좀 softens the request; -아/어 주세요 'please do for me'.
nuance: 요금제 (料金制, literally '料金 fee/charge + 制 system' = 'fee system/plan') is a mobile-phone service pricing plan — the package of data, calls, and texts you sign up for — and it is one of the first words a newcomer needs when getting a phone. The crucial contrast is 요금제 (the plan/scheme) vs 요금 (料金, the fee/charge itself): 요금제를 바꿨어요 = I changed my PLAN, but 요금이 많이 나왔어요 = the CHARGE came out high (my bill was big). Confusing them is the main pitfall. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 요금제를 바꾸다/고르다/선택하다, 요금제가 비싸다/싸다, 요금제를 추천하다, and feature names like 데이터 무제한 요금제, 알뜰 요금제 (budget/MVNO plan). Particle note: when switching, the new plan is the destination with 으로 — 새 요금제로 바꾸다, not 요금제를 바꾸다 alone when you mean 'switch TO'. The 알뜰폰 (budget carrier) world is where newcomers often hunt for a cheap 요금제.

Treating 요금제 as a generic 'price'. It specifically means a telecom service plan, not the price of goods (that's 가격 or 값).

usage: 연락(連絡)하다 'get in touch'; 문자로 = by text. After a vowel the means particle is plain 로, and 문자 ends in the vowel ㅏ, so 문자로, never 문자으로.
오다 'come' is the natural verb for an incoming message; 문자가 왔어요 = a text arrived.
보내다 'send'; the send/receive pair is 보내다 / 받다, and incoming ones 오다.
확인(確認)하다 'confirm/check'; you 확인하다 a message you received.
examples: 문자가 왔어요.
A text came in.
Incoming messages use 오다 (come), not 받다, in this announcing sense: 문자가 왔어요.
은행에서 문자가 왔어요.
A text came from the bank.
에서 marks the source 'from' (an organization); the bank as origin of the text.
주소를 문자로 보내 주세요.
Please send the address by text.
Means 문자로 'by text'; -아/어 주세요 for a polite request.
nuance: 문자 (文字, 'written character/letter') in daily speech is the everyday word for an SMS text message — short for 문자 메시지. The pitfall is its double life: literally 문자 means written characters/letters (e.g. 한글은 한국의 문자예요, 'Hangul is Korea's writing system'), so context decides. Crucially, 문자 is NOT a paper letter in the mail — that is 편지 (便紙). The near-synonym 카톡 (a KakaoTalk message) is what most people actually send now; 문자 specifically implies the carrier SMS (often bank/official notices), while a casual chat is 카톡 or 메시지. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 문자를 보내다/받다, 문자가 오다, 문자를 확인하다, 문자로 연락하다, and the source pattern 은행/회사에서 문자가 오다. Particle traps: 'by text' is 문자로 (means); the sender/source is marked 에서 for organizations (은행에서) or 한테서/에게서 for people. English speakers often want 'text' as a verb — Korean splits it into 문자를 보내다 (send a text).

Forgetting 문자 needs a verb for 'to text'. There is no single verb; say 문자를 보내다 (send a text) or 문자로 연락하다 (contact by text).

usage: Means 으로; 영상통화로 = by/over video call. 이야기하다 'talk/chat'.
통화 is a 하다-noun, so the action is 영상통화를 하다 'do a video call', i.e. make one.
끊기다 'be cut off (passive)'; a bad connection 끊겨요. Contrast 끊다 'hang up (on purpose)'.
연결(連結) 'connection'; 안 되다 'fails to work' — a frequent complaint with weak signal.
examples: 가족이랑 영상통화를 해요.
I video-call with my family.
이랑 'with' (casual) marks the other party; the action is 영상통화를 하다.
영상통화로 얼굴 보면서 이야기해요.
We talk while seeing each other's faces on video call.
-면서 'while (doing both)'; the appeal of video is 얼굴을 보다 (see the face).
주말에 부모님이랑 영상통화를 했어요.
I video-called my parents on the weekend.
Time 에 (주말에) + companion 이랑; past 했어요.
nuance: 영상통화 (映像通話, '映像 video-image + 通話 phone-call' = literally 'video phone call') is a phone call with live video — invaluable for newcomers keeping in touch with family abroad. The sharp contrast is with plain 통화 (通話), a voice-only call: 그냥 통화 = a normal voice call, but 영상통화 = with video, so dropping 영상 changes the meaning. Don't say just 통화 when you specifically mean seeing each other's faces. The near-synonym 화상통화 exists (more formal/business, e.g. video conferencing leans 화상 회의), while 영상통화 is the everyday personal term, and people also say 페이스타임/영통 casually. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 영상통화를 하다, 영상통화로 이야기하다/얼굴을 보다, 영상통화가 끊기다, and 영상통화 연결이 안 되다. Particle/verb traps: it is a 하다-noun, so 'make a video call' = 영상통화를 하다 (not 영상통화하다 in writing, though spoken); the other party takes 이랑/하고/와/과 ('with'); 'over video call' is 영상통화로.

mistakes: Dropping 영상 and saying just 통화 when you mean a video call. 통화 alone is a voice call; keep 영상 (or say 영상통화) for video.
Using 끊다 instead of 끊기다 for a dropped call. 끊다 = you deliberately hang up; 끊기다 = it got cut off by itself (bad signal). '전화가 끊겼어요' = the call dropped.
Marking the other person with 에게/한테 as if calling 'to' them. The companion in a video call takes 와/과/하고/이랑 ('with'): 친구랑 영상통화를 해요.

usage: to make a photo into wallpaper
바꾸다 'change/swap'; the most common action — 배경화면을 자주 바꿔요.
설정(設定)하다 'set/configure'; 으로 marks the role 'as' — 사진을 배경화면으로 설정하다.
Related: 잠금(lock)+화면(screen). The lock screen is 잠금화면, the home/background is 배경화면.
examples: 배경화면이 예뻐요.
The wallpaper is pretty.
예쁘다 (pretty) is a ㅡ-irregular → 예뻐요 (the ㅡ drops before 어).
강아지 사진으로 배경화면을 바꿨어요.
I changed my wallpaper to a dog photo.
Material 으로 'with (a dog photo)'; past 바꿨어요.
이 사진을 배경화면으로 설정했어요.
I set this photo as my wallpaper.
Role 으로 'as'; 설정하다 is the menu-style verb for 'set/apply'.
nuance: 배경화면 (背景畫面, '背景 background + 畫面 screen-picture' = 'background screen image') is the wallpaper/background image on a phone or computer — and the pitfall is the English word 'wallpaper': this is purely the digital screen background, never the paper you put on a real room wall. Room wallpaper is 벽지 (壁紙, 'wall-paper'), so '방 배경화면을 발랐어요' would be nonsense — you 벽지를 바르다 (paste wallpaper) on a wall. Within screens, contrast 배경화면 (the home/background image) with 잠금화면 (lock screen) and 바탕화면 (the desktop on a computer); they overlap but name different surfaces. The component 화면 (畫面) means 'screen/display', the same 화면 as in 모니터 화면. Register is neutral. Habitual collocations: 배경화면을 바꾸다/설정하다, 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면이 예쁘다/어둡다, and the pair 배경화면/잠금화면. Particle note: the photo you use is the material/role with 으로 — 사진으로 배경화면을 만들다, 배경화면으로 설정하다.
